extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) prosecuting pre‑AIA patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying and overcoming rejections under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) (novelty/prior art) in patent examination, including definitions of statutory terms, evidentiary standards, and procedural remedies (affidavits/declarations, claim amendments, priority/benefit claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) statutory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 — Conditions for patentability; novelty and loss of right to patent. A person shall be entitled to a patent unless - (a) the invention was known or used by others in this country, or patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country, before the invention thereof by the applicant for a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Known or Used” means publicly known or used
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory language 'known or used by others in this country' means knowledge or use which is accessible to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accessibility requires no deliberate attempt to keep it secret. See Carella v. Starlight Archery and W.L. Gore v. Garlock; see MPEP §2128–§2128.02 for case law concerning public accessibility of publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of product made by secret process — public use test
rubrics_metrics.description: The nonsecret use of a claimed process in the usual course of producing articles for commercial purposes is a public use. Secret use of the process coupled with sale of the product does not result in public use of the process unless the public could learn the claimed process by examining the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, secret use of a process by another, even if the product is commercially sold, cannot result in a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) if an examination of the product would not reveal the process. (Cited authority in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: “In this country” means within the United States only
rubrics_metrics.description: Only knowledge or use in the U.S. can be used in a pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior knowledge or use not present in the United States, even if widespread in a foreign country, cannot be the basis of a pre‑AIA 102(a) rejection. Changes by NAFTA/URAA do not alter the meaning for purposes of pre‑AIA 102(a). (See In re Ekenstam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: “By others” — meaning of the term
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'others' in pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) refers to any entity which is different from the inventive entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entity need only differ by one person to be 'by others'. This applies to all types of references (publications, public knowledge/use). Any other interpretation would negate the one‑year grace period afforded under §102(b). (See In re Katz.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents and publications (domestic/foreign) as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference 'patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country' can be used as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2126 for information on the use of secret patents as prior art and rules on dates/availability of patents as references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection by one or more specified means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated methods (from MPEP): (A) Persuasively argue that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) Amend the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) File an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing prior invention, if the reference is not a U.S. patent or a U.S. patent application publication claiming interfering subject matter (see MPEP §715 and note that 1.131 is not appropriate when the reference is a U.S. patent/application publication directed to same invention or obvious variants); (D) File an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing that the reference invention is not by 'another' (i.e., that the reference's disclosure was derived from the inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work); (E) Submit and perfect a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a); (F) Submit and perfect a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or 120 (see MPEP §§216 and 211 et seq.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing reference’s disclosure was derived from the inventor (derivation/declared authorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case is made under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) if, within 1 year of the filing date, the invention (or an obvious variant) is described in a printed publication whose authorship differs in any way from the inventive entity unless the publication itself states it is describing the inventor's or a joint inventor's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor's or joint inventor's disclosure of his/her own work within the year before filing cannot be used as prior art against the application. If a co‑author is listed on a cited publication but the inventor or a joint inventor can show the publication originated with or was obtained from the inventor, the publication may be removed by filing disclaiming affidavits by other authors or a specific declaration by the inventor/joint inventor. A mere naked assertion of inventorship in a 1.132 declaration is insufficient; declarations must provide context, explanation, or evidence (see EmeraChem v. Volkswagen). If a co‑author refuses to disclaim inventorship and provides evidence to the contrary, the inventor's affidavit may be insufficient and the rejection may stand. It is possible to add coauthors as joint inventors if requirements of 35 U.S.C. 116 (third paragraph) are met. Case examples: In re Katz; Ex parte Hirschler; Ex parte Kroger; In re Searles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 37 CFR 1.131 affidavits to antedate references
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference is not a statutory bar under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), (c), or (d), an applicant can overcome a rejection by swearing back of the reference through submission of an affidavit under 37 CFR 1.131.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference discloses the inventor's or a joint inventor's own work as derived from the inventor/joint inventor, either a 1.131 affidavit to antedate the reference or a 1.132 affidavit to show derivation and invention by the inventor/joint inventor may be submitted. See In re Foster and In re Facius. See MPEP §715 for more information on evidentiary requirements and when 1.131 can be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements and limits on affidavits/declarations (evidentiary sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations (37 CFR 1.131, 1.132) used to overcome prior‑art rejections must provide sufficient evidence and context; bare or naked assertions are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration that is only a naked assertion of inventorship and fails to provide any context, explanation, or evidence will be insufficient to show the relied‑upon subject matter was the inventor's own work (EmeraChem v. Volkswagen). If evidence exists that co‑authors dispute inventorship, a single inventor's declaration may not suffice. See MPEP §715 and cited case law for examples and required supporting evidence.
